paper.title: What Stops Recursive Self-Improvement in Robotics? Lessons from 123 Rounds of Agentic Skill Discovery
paper.central_claim: In a 123-round run of an agentic robot self-improvement loop (GPT coding agents in Codex CLI proposing skill code or external models, accepted only after physical simulation tests, with humans allowed to repair only the testing harness), the agent can discover missing capabilities (e.g. active viewing) but its accepted changes did not add up: the target RoboCasa Fridge task never succeeded. The agent was rarely the bottleneck; three surrounding factors were: (1) chained perception modules do not represent relations so the agent displaces semantics into ever-growing geometric code, (2) skill chains lock learning onto the first failing step, (3) the harness (evaluators, gates, memory, embodiment description) decides what is learned.
paper.claim_scope_note: Negative-result / diagnostic report of one long run: one simulator (RoboCasa), one kitchen layout, three tasks, no independent replicates or ablations (authors' own limitation); recommendations D1-D12 are untested hypotheses.
paper.scope_decision: in_scope (A-class): embodied harness self-optimisation; GPT coding agents revise robot skill code/providers with simulator gates; negative-result report evaluated against its own central claims.

initial_evidence_judgment: Read before seat totals: one 123-round run of a Codex-CLI GPT agent loop improving RoboCasa skills under human-only harness repair. Central outcome (no target success, Fridge 0/486) is natively measured with complete counts; three diagnoses (relational perception displacement, frontier lock, harness capture) are supported by detailed trace statistics but are observational, confounded by co-changing harness/models/providers; "agent rarely the bottleneck" untested; remedies untested. Type: a system run with negative closed-loop findings (system_method). Expect online, scoped.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: Closed-loop RoboCasa simulation with native task success and complete denominators; no transfer evidence or claim.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: In one 123-round run of a GPT-agent-driven robot self-improvement loop on RoboCasa kitchen tasks, 57 accepted skill changes and 86 model registrations yielded no success on the target Fridge task (0/486) and only mostly accidental Sink successes, and the recorded failures trace to relational perception, chain-length frontier lock, and evaluator/gate/memory defects that humans repaired 113 times; whether a different agent or budget would change this, and whether the proposed fixes work, are untested.

assessment.reproduction_note: All results author-reported; nothing run by us.

G.reason: Specific, important question (do agent-made robot improvements compound and what stops them) located against named neighbours (Voyager, Eureka, DGM; RHO, ASPIRE, ENPIRE) with an explicit account of why those settings satisfy the three conditions by construction, and a residual explicitly bounded in §10 (one run, no controls, untested remedies). Anchor 4; the neighbour characterisation is the authors' reading, which is acceptable for problem location.

M.reason: Chain model S=prod p_j with Delta S = pi_j Delta p_j prod p_i and the representability/expressibility/resolvability account map each failure to a mechanism and come with falsifying experiments (Table 3). Not 4: the framework is diagnostic and fitted to one run; relative importance of the bottlenecks is untested (both seats).

X.reason: Roles, information per agent, model/effort schedule, caps, gate sequence, human-repair rule and a round-by-round record make the run largely reconstructible. Not 4: the selection side changed through 113 harness repairs whose concrete thresholds and step-evaluator predicates are mostly named rather than specified, and prompts/code are not shown, so the selection rule in force at a given round cannot be fully rebuilt.

measurement.reason: The central negative outcome rests on native RoboCasa task success with complete per-task counts (Fridge 0/486, Cabinet 0/256, Sink 14/230 with 9 accidental), evaluator capture is detected and quantified, accidental successes are separated. Not 4: step-level diagnostics use privileged step evaluators that were buggy and repeatedly changed, effective n is four deterministic seeds per task, and "out-of-view failures disappeared" is partly contradicted by later target_not_in_view rows.

causality.reason: Mechanisms are dissected with counts, but harness repairs, agent models/effort and providers changed together and the central "agent was rarely the bottleneck" is not tested by varying agent, compute or representation (authors concede). Anchor 2 (both seats).

holdout.reason: Reported tasks are the development tasks on four fixed seeds with task-level gain ~0, exactly anchor 2; a held-out task existed for gating but was visible before round 74. Claims are honestly scoped in §10 (one simulator, layout, three tasks), so the negative result is not inflated; the title-level generalisation is not tested.

statistics.reason: Failure denominators are unusually complete (first-failed step distribution, per-seed endpoints, attempt/rejection counts, 16/36 re-run pairs not reproducing), but the loop is a single run with no replicates and no CI/variance on rates. Anchor v2 (binding): trial counts without variance/CI -> 1-2; the complete failure decomposition puts it at 2.

cost.reason: Wall time (1-3 h per round, several weeks), 847 attempts with per-attempt caps (3 x 60 min) and 113 human repairs make the agent call budget roughly inferable, but no token, USD or GPU totals are given and the privileged-evaluator/provider compute is not priced; this is the anchor-2 case (call budget inferable, privileged channel not priced).

resolutions.reason: Problem location, lineage and explicitly bounded residual meet anchor 4; sol's only reason (originals not independently compared) applies to every paper in the batch and is not a problem-location defect here.

The selection side (evaluators, gates, thresholds) changed through 113 repairs that are mostly named, not specified, and the paper's own Lesson 3 depends on them; prompts/code absent. Reconstruction of the selection/retention rule per round is incomplete, below anchor 4.

The v2 caps do not bind: the native task criterion is defined and every denominator is complete, results are not single-trial. Step-evaluator defects and effective n=4 seeds keep it below 4; sol's concern applies to step diagnostics, not to the central native outcome.
Literal anchor-2 case (development tasks evaluated, gain ~0); a negative result on dev tasks is not inflated by overlap, and the claims are scoped honestly in §10.
Anchor v2 (binding for a2): trial counts without variance/CI -> 1-2; one unreplicated loop run. Complete failure decomposition earns the top of that band, not 3.

Not a midpoint: the evidence matches the anchor-2 description exactly (call budget inferable from 847 attempts x caps and round wall-time; privileged evaluator/provider compute and tokens/USD unpriced). Sol undercounts the inferable budget; son55 credits as disclosed what is only bounded.

K401 revises the harness around a frozen agent, but here only humans may change the harness (the paper's point); the agent revises robot skill code between rounds with model-free deployment, which is R05. K303 kept as partial for the skill library.
